title: Kenyan Masala Chai
community: Enjoyed across all Kenyan communities — the national drink
author: Mama Wanjiru

heritage.origin: Indian-Kenyan tradition — now Kenya's definitive national beverage
heritage.history: Chai has been drunk across Kenya for over a century, introduced by Indian communities who settled during the colonial period. Over generations it evolved into something distinctly Kenyan — stronger tea, more ginger, boiled directly with milk rather than steeped separately, and always sweetened generously. Today, Kenyan masala chai is recognised internationally as one of the world's great spiced teas.
heritage.modernEvolution: Now exported as a concept worldwide, Kenyan chai is the base for numerous commercial chai products. At home, it remains made the same way it always has been — directly on the stove, with real spices.

desc: Kenyan Masala Chai is Kenya's national drink — black tea boiled directly with fresh ginger, whole spices, and milk, then strained and sweetened. Bold, warming, fragrant, and deeply comforting. The beverage that accompanies every Kenyan breakfast, every gathering, and every conversation.
longDesc: There is no more universally Kenyan experience than being handed a cup of hot, sweet, spiced chai. From the highlands to the coast, from roadside kiosks to corporate boardrooms, chai is the constant. The Kenyan method — boiling tea directly with milk and spices rather than steeping separately — produces a uniquely strong, fragrant, deeply flavoured result that no tea bag in hot water can approach.
ingredients: 3 tsp loose black tea leaves (or 3 tea bags)
2 tsp sugar — or more to taste
2cm piece fresh ginger — sliced or grated

substitutions.alternative: Evaporated milk for a richer result — very popular in Kenya
3—4 tea bags — Ketepa or any Kenyan black tea is ideal

steps: Combine water, ginger, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, and peppercorns in a small saucepan.
Bring to a boil over medium heat. Boil for 2—3 minutes to extract the spice flavours.
Add the tea leaves or tea bags. Boil for 1 minute.
Bring back to a boil, stirring — watch carefully as milk boils over quickly.
Reduce heat and simmer for 2—3 minutes until the chai has deepened in colour and flavour.
Strain through a fine mesh strainer into cups.
chefTips: Boiling the spices in water first before adding tea and milk extracts the maximum flavour.
Never walk away from the stove once milk is added — it boils over in seconds.
The longer the chai simmers after adding milk, the stronger and more fragrant it becomes.
Kenyan chai should be properly sweet — do not be shy with the sugar.
commonMistakes: Not boiling long enough — weak, pale chai.
Walking away when milk is in the pan — it overflows.
Under-sweetening — authentic Kenyan chai is generously sweetened.

faqs.q: What tea is best for Kenyan chai?
faqs.a: Kenyan black tea — particularly Ketepa brand — is the authentic choice. It is a strong, full-bodied tea that stands up to the spices and milk. Assam or any strong black tea works as a substitute.

faqs.q: Can I make it without dairy?
faqs.a: Yes — use full-fat oat milk or coconut milk. Coconut milk gives a distinctly coastal character.

cookingScience: Boiling tea with milk extracts different compounds than steeping in water alone. The milk proteins interact with tannins in the tea, binding some of the astringency and producing a smoother, rounder flavour than water-steeped tea. This is why Kenyan boiled chai tastes categorically different from a tea bag in a mug.
sustainabilityTips: Kenya is one of the world's great tea-producing countries — buy Kenyan tea to support local farmers.
Used tea leaves can be composted.
storage: Best drunk fresh. Can be refrigerated for 1 day and reheated.
reheating: Warm gently in a saucepan — do not boil vigorously or it becomes bitter.
healthBenefits: Black tea is rich in polyphenols and antioxidants.
Ginger has anti-inflammatory and digestive properties.
Cardamom supports digestion and has antimicrobial properties.
Cinnamon helps regulate blood sugar levels.
culturalNote: Kenyan Masala Chai is not just a drink — it is a social institution. No Kenyan meeting begins without it, no guest goes unserved, and no morning is complete without a cup. It is the thread that runs through every conversation, gathering, and quiet moment in Kenyan daily life.
regionalVariations: Classic Kenyan masala chai with ginger and cardamom.
Coastal chai — with extra cardamom and sometimes coconut milk.
Lemon ginger chai — with a squeeze of lemon.
Strong kiosk chai — the roadside version, extra strong and very sweet.
Light afternoon chai — less tea, more milk.
